passage:
Monday. Dolma lined up chairs for a bus. Her mother Farida said, "Let's make it a train with a whistle!" Dolma's face fell and she wandered off to her blocks.
Wednesday. Farida sat on the floor and asked, "What can I be?" "A passenger with a big bag," Dolma said, and told her where to sit.
Saturday. Dolma announced, "Today the bus goes to Nani's, and you are sleepy." Farida yawned and nodded, and Dolma beamed from the driver's seat.

qa.q: Where does the bus go on Saturday?
qa.a: It goes to Nani's.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when her face fell on Monday?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and overruled, because her mother turned her bus into a train.

qa.q: What turning point helped Farida and Dolma enjoy the game?
qa.a: On Wednesday Farida asked what she could be instead of directing, and took the small role Dolma gave her.

qa.q: What might Farida notice about Dolma from Wednesday to Saturday?
qa.a: She may notice Dolma growing confident and pleased, giving orders and inventing the story herself.

grounding: A parent who follows the child's lead and takes a small role gives the child authority in play.

passage:
The lights went out with the thunder, and Ritu decided the sofa was a rocket.
"Mama, you're the space cat," she said, handing Salma a torch. "Cats don't talk."
Salma wanted to check the dal, but she got down on the floor instead, a dupatta for a tail. "Meow?"
"No! You wait for orders." Ritu pointed at the ceiling. "Ten, nine, eight..."
Lightning cracked. Ritu gripped the sofa arm, and the cat crept close and stayed quiet, just as the captain had ordered. "Blast off," said Ritu, and grinned at her cat.

qa.q: What did Ritu decide the sofa was?
qa.a: She decided it was a rocket.

qa.q: What might Ritu feel when the lightning cracks?
qa.a: She is a little frightened but trying to stay brave. She grips the sofa arm, and the cat stays close and quiet.

qa.q: What choice did Salma make that helped in the storm?
qa.a: She left the dal and took the small role of the space cat, following Ritu's rules and staying close.

qa.q: How might Salma see the game during the power cut?
qa.a: She may see it as a way to keep Ritu calm and happy, since she gives up her own plans and enjoys the story.

grounding: A parent takes a small role in a child's pretend play and lets the child write the story.

passage:
On the floor of their Pune flat, Mridul had built a zoo out of cushions. His mother, Kalyani, came to sit beside him with her tea. "What can I be?"
Mridul thought hard. "You're the elephant. But you have to stay in the cushion house."
Kalyani set down the tea, went down on her knees and swung her arm like a trunk. "Like this?"
"No, softer. Elephants are gentle." She made it softer. Mridul fed her a pretend banana and announced that visiting hours were over. He was grinning so hard his cheeks shone.

qa.q: What role did Mridul give his mother?
qa.a: The elephant, who had to stay in the cushion house.

qa.q: What does Mridul's big grin suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt proud and delighted to be in charge, with his mother enjoying his game.

qa.q: What did Kalyani do that made the play work?
qa.a: She asked "What can I be?", took the small role, and made her trunk softer when Mridul asked.

qa.q: What would change if Kalyani had started directing the zoo?
qa.a: Mridul might have lost the feeling of being in charge and enjoyed, and the zoo would have become her story.

grounding: Shows a parent following a child's lead in play by taking a small role and letting the child run the story.

passage:
"Amma, you're the student. Sit there." Lakshmi pointed her mother, Mahima, to the floor mat.
Mahima sat. "Yes, Teacher."
"Today we learn the letter M. Write it."
Mahima wrote a wobbly M on the slate. "Is this right, Teacher?"
"Hmm." Lakshmi frowned exactly like her class teacher. "Too big. Try again."
"Okay." Mahima tried again, smaller.
"Good! You get a star." Lakshmi drew a star on Mahima's hand.
"Teacher, can I go to the toilet?"
"No, first finish." Then Lakshmi burst out laughing. "Okay, you can go."
Mahima laughed too, and stayed exactly where she was.

qa.q: Which letter did Lakshmi teach?
qa.a: The letter M.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi burst out laughing?
qa.a: She was delighted and enjoying being in charge, and found her own strictness funny.

qa.q: How did Mahima let Lakshmi lead?
qa.a: She took the student role, followed every instruction and asked permission, letting Lakshmi make the rules.

qa.q: What might Mahima be enjoying about being the student?
qa.a: Mahima gets to see how Lakshmi sees her class teacher, and to share her daughter's delight.

grounding: Shows a parent taking the small role of student and letting the child lead the pretend class.

passage:
Parent play morning, Nursery B, Saturday.
Hansa's father joined her at the sand table. At first he started building a castle himself, and Hansa went quiet, watching. Then he stopped and asked her, "What's this place going to be?" She said, "A river town. You're the boat man." He took the little wooden boat and waited for instructions. For twenty minutes he pushed the boat wherever she pointed, and she talked non-stop, naming the shops and the houses.
When he left, she told me, "Papa listened to my story."
Next step: share this with other parents. Ask first, then take the small role.
Rehana

qa.q: What role did Hansa give her father?
qa.a: The boat man.

qa.q: Why did Hansa go quiet at first?
qa.a: She probably felt left out and deflated when her father started building his own castle.

qa.q: What turned the play around?
qa.a: He stopped building, asked "What's this place going to be?", and followed her directions with the boat.

qa.q: How does Rehana plan to use what happened?
qa.a: Rehana plans to share it with other parents: ask the child first, then take the small role.

grounding: Shows a parent switching from directing play to following the child's lead, and the child feeling listened to.

passage:
In the village courtyard, Pooja had set up a tea stall with three clay cups and a tin can for a kettle.
"Amma, you be the customer."
Vinita wanted to show her how a real stall works. She didn't. She sat on the step instead. "One tea, please."
"Sugar?"
"Yes, please."
"No sugar today. Only salt tea," said Pooja, very firmly.
"Oh! Then salt tea, please."
Pooja poured air into a cup and handed it over with great care. Vinita pretended to sip. "Very good tea."
Pooja beamed. "Next customer!" she called to the goat.

qa.q: How many clay cups did Pooja have?
qa.a: Pooja had three clay cups.

qa.q: How did Pooja feel when Vinita praised the tea?
qa.a: Pooja felt proud and delighted, beaming as the one running the stall.

qa.q: Which choice of Vinita's helped Pooja, and why?
qa.a: Vinita held back from directing and played the customer, even accepting salt tea, so Pooja stayed in charge of the story.

qa.q: What would change if Vinita had rearranged the stall her own way?
qa.a: Pooja might feel less in charge and less enjoyed, and the game would become Vinita's instead of hers.

grounding: A parent follows the child's lead in play, taking a small role, and the child feels in charge and enjoyed.
